title: The Hidden Isosceles Triangle | AMC 8-Style Level 4

scenes.visual: Figure from the bank SVG (triangle ABC, parallel line through A, segment BF) draws itself. On line 2 the triangle ABF glows green for a beat (no length shown yet). Line 3: Vantee title card.
lines: This question gives you three side lengths. You only need one of them.
Hiding in the picture is a special triangle. Once you spot it, the answer pops right out.
Hi, I'm Vantee! Let's go triangle hunting.

scenes.visual: Question text top-left (KaTeX), the figure on the right, large, with labels A, B, C, F and side lengths 10, 10, 12 at 48px+. Lines: highlight AB and AC (line 2), BC (line 2), draw the parallel line (line 3), draw BF as the bisector (line 4). Line 6: five choice chips 5, 6, 8, 10, 12.
lines: Here's the question.
Triangle A B C has A B and A C both equal to ten, and B C equal to twelve.
A line through point A runs parallel to B C.
The line that cuts angle A B C exactly in half meets this line at point F.
How long is A F?
Here are the five choices. Take a good look.

scenes.visual: Figure only. Line 1: the top line and BC get matching parallel arrow marks. Line 2: angle at B split by BF into two equal angles, both marked with the same purple arc. Line 3: segment AF pulses with a '?' label above it.
lines: So what do we know? The top line and B C never meet. They're parallel.
The line from B to F splits the corner at B into two equal angles. That's what bisector means.
We want the length of A F, the piece of the top line from A to F.

scenes.visual: Pause card with countdown ring; the question figure stays visible, dimmed.
lines: Now it's your turn. Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!

scenes.visual: Figure on the left, angle notes on a right panel. Line 2: angle ABF and angle FBC both get a purple arc labeled x. Line 3: highlight the Z shape: BF crossing the two parallel lines, angle FBC (bottom) and angle AFB (top, at F) glow together. Line 4: angle AFB gets a purple arc labeled x. Panel rows: 'angle ABF = x', 'angle FBC = x', 'angle AFB = x'.
lines: Welcome back! Here's the strategy: chase the angles.
The bisector splits angle B into two equal parts. Let's call each part x.
Now look for a Z shape. The line B F crosses the two parallel lines.
Inside a Z, the two corner angles are equal. So the angle at F is also x!

scenes.visual: Triangle ABF fills green (soft). Its two angles marked x at B and at F glow. Line 2: sides AB and AF get matching tick marks. Line 3: AB label 10 slides/copies onto AF. Line 4: Answer badge 'AF = 10' with chime at end of line; choice D highlighted.
lines: Now look at triangle A B F. It has two equal angles, both x.
A triangle with two equal angles has two equal sides, the sides opposite those angles.
Side A F sits across from the angle at B. Side A B sits across from the angle at F. So A F equals A B.
A B is ten, so A F is ten. That's Choice D!

scenes.visual: Same figure. Mark point G on BC with BG = 10 (label 10 under BG). Mark a spot on the top line 10 from A (it coincides with F; show it first as a dot, F label fading in only at the end). Draw the four-sided shape A-B-G-spot, shade it; label all four sides 10 with tick marks. Draw diagonal from B to the spot, with two equal angle arcs at B; the bisector line overlays it exactly; then the label F appears. Finish with a small card 'bisector + parallel line → isosceles triangle'.
lines: Here's another way to see it. Let's build a shape.
Mark a point G on B C so that B G is ten, the same as A B.
Now mark the spot ten along the top line from A. Let's check that the bisector lands exactly there.
Join it up with A, B and G. The top and bottom are parallel and both ten.
Parallel and equal top and bottom make a parallelogram, so the slanted sides match too.
That's ten and ten. All four sides are ten. A rhombus!
A rhombus's diagonal cuts its corner exactly in half.
So the bisector from B goes right through that spot. It's F, ten from A. Same answer!
When would you pick this way? When you'd rather build a shape than chase angles. Both work!

scenes.visual: Choice chips row; each wrong chip turns red with a short reason as it's discussed. Line 2: half of BC highlighted (6). Line 3: BC highlighted (12). Line 4: dashed altitude from A down to BC labeled 8, with the 6-8-10 right triangle shaded. Line 5: AB halved (5). Line 6: the 10 chip green.
lines: Now let's look at the wrong answers. Each one is a trap.
Choice B, six, is half of B C. That's a real length in the picture, but not A F.
Choice E, twelve, is B C itself. A F is parallel to B C, but it isn't the same length.
Choice C, eight, is the height of the triangle, from A straight down to B C. That's a real length, but the wrong one.
Choice A, five, is what you'd get if you cut A B in half.
So here's a great habit. When you see a bisector and a parallel line, look for an isosceles triangle.

scenes.visual: New figure: triangle with B at left, C at right, BC = 10 at the bottom, AB = 7, AC = 9 (A computed from these lengths, NOT isosceles), the parallel line through A extending right, the bisector from B meeting it at F to the right of A. Labels 7, 9, 10 at 48px+.
lines: Ready for a challenge? This triangle is lopsided.
A B is seven, A C is nine, and B C is ten.
Again, a line through A runs parallel to B C, and the bisector of angle B meets it at F.
How long is A F this time?

scenes.visual: Pause card, countdown, variant figure visible.
lines: Pause the video, and go for it!

scenes.visual: Variant figure. Line 1: two equal x arcs at B. Line 2: Z shape glows, x arc at F. Line 3: triangle ABF shaded green, tick marks on AB and AF. Line 4: answer badge 'AF = 7' with chime. Line 5: the 9 and 10 labels fade to grey.
lines: Let's check. The bisector splits angle B into two equal angles, x and x.
The Z shape across the parallel lines makes the angle at F equal x too.
So triangle A B F has two equal angles, and A F equals A B.
So the length of A F is seven!
Here's the sneaky part. The nine and the ten didn't matter at all. If you got seven, well done!

scenes.visual: Clean summary card: small diagram of the pattern (parallel lines, bisector, the green isosceles triangle with two x angles and matching ticks) and the rule text.
lines: Here's the big idea to remember.
A parallel line makes Z angles equal.
So when a bisector crosses a parallel line, look for a triangle with two equal angles. Two of its sides match!
I'm Vantee. Keep exploring, and I'll see you next time!
